question.title: Creating Projects
question.scenario: A team lead needs to set up a new GCP environment for a development team. They need to organize resources, set up billing, and ensure proper access controls.
question.question-text: Which gcloud command creates a new GCP project?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about which top-level gcloud command group handles project lifecycle operations. The verb follows the resource noun directly in gcloud's command structure.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The correct command is "gcloud projects create PROJECT_ID", which creates a new GCP project. Option A incorrectly nests projects under the compute group, which is only for Compute Engine resources. Option B uses "new" which is not a valid gcloud verb. Option C uses "init" which is reserved for SDK initialization, not project creation. You can optionally pass --name for a human-readable display name, --organization or --folder to place the project in a resource hierarchy, and --labels for tagging.

ul.li: Project IDs must be globally unique across all of Google Cloud, are 6-30 characters, and cannot be changed after creation. Choose carefully since deletion only releases the ID after 30 days.
The project creator automatically receives the Owner role (roles/owner), which grants full administrative access. In organizations, this can be modified by org policies.
A project cannot consume paid GCP services until linked to an active billing account via gcloud billing projects link.
Most GCP APIs are disabled by default on new projects and must be explicitly enabled with gcloud services enable before resources can be created.

question.title: Managing Billing Accounts
question.scenario: A finance administrator needs to link a newly created project to the company's billing account to enable resource creation.
question.question-text: What permission is required to link a project to a billing account?

choices.choice: Only Project Owner on the project
Billing Account User on the billing account AND Project Owner or Editor on the project

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Linking billing is a cross-resource operation that touches two distinct GCP resources. Consider what permissions you would need on each side of that link.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Linking a project to a billing account requires permissions on both resources: Billing Account User (roles/billing.user) on the billing account to authorize its use, AND Project Owner or Editor on the project to modify its billing settings. Option A fails because project-level permissions alone cannot authorize use of a billing account you have no access to. Option B fails because billing admin can manage the account itself but cannot modify project settings. Option D is wrong because Organization Administrator is not a billing-specific role and alone does not satisfy either requirement.

ul.li: Billing Account Administrator (roles/billing.admin) can manage the billing account, create sub-accounts, and view costs, but cannot link projects unless they also have project-level permissions. This is a common exam trick.
Billing Account User (roles/billing.user) is intentionally narrow: it only allows linking projects to the billing account. It cannot view invoices, modify payment methods, or manage budgets.
Projects without a linked billing account can only use free-tier resources. Attempting to create paid resources returns a billing-not-enabled error.
Billing export to BigQuery (via billing account settings) enables granular cost analysis with SQL queries, and is the recommended approach for enterprise cost management and chargeback reporting.

question.title: Deploying Compute Engine Instances
question.scenario: A developer needs to deploy a web server with specific machine type, boot disk, and network tags for firewall rules.
question.question-text: Which gcloud command creates a VM instance with a custom machine type and specific boot disk?

choices.choice: gcloud compute instances create with --machine-type and --boot-disk-size flags
gcloud compute vm new with --machine and --boot flags
gcloud instances deploy with --type and --storage flags
gcloud vm create with --size and --disk flags

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: How does gcloud typically structure commands for creating a specific resource type? Think about which command group VMs belong to and how flag names relate to the properties being set.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The correct command is "gcloud compute instances create INSTANCE_NAME --machine-type=TYPE --boot-disk-size=SIZE". Options A, B, and C all use fabricated command groups and flag names that do not exist in the gcloud CLI. The real gcloud compute instances create command supports --zone for placement, --image-family for OS selection, --tags for network tags used by firewall rules, --metadata for startup scripts, and --service-account for the VM's identity. Understanding the correct flag names is critical for the exam since distractors often use plausible-sounding but invalid alternatives.

ul.li: Custom machine types use --custom-cpu and --custom-memory flags (e.g., --custom-cpu=4 --custom-memory=16GB), allowing precise resource allocation without being locked into predefined machine families like n2-standard or e2-medium.

The --metadata-from-file flag loads startup scripts from local files (e.g., --metadata-from-file=startup-script=init.sh), while --metadata passes inline values. Startup scripts run on every boot unless you use startup-script-url for remote scripts.
Preemptible VMs (--preemptible) and Spot VMs (--provisioning-model=SPOT) cost 60-91% less but can be terminated at any time. Spot VMs are the newer replacement with more flexible eviction policies.
The --deletion-protection flag prevents accidental VM deletion via Console or CLI. It must be explicitly removed before the instance can be deleted, providing a safety net for production workloads.

question.title: SSH Access to VMs
question.scenario: An engineer needs to connect to a Compute Engine VM for troubleshooting but the VM only has an internal IP address.
question.question-text: What is the recommended way to SSH to a VM without an external IP address?

choices.choice: SSH is not possible without external IP
Always assign an external IP for SSH access
Use Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) TCP forwarding with gcloud compute ssh --tunnel-through-iap
Use Cloud NAT for inbound SSH

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Does SSH strictly require a public IP, or does GCP offer a way to reach internal-only VMs through an identity-aware tunnel?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) TCP forwarding tunnels SSH connections through Google's infrastructure to VMs that only have internal IPs. The command "gcloud compute ssh INSTANCE --tunnel-through-iap" establishes this secure connection. Option A is wrong because IAP makes SSH fully functional without external IPs. Option B is a security anti-pattern since exposing VMs publicly increases the attack surface. Option D is incorrect because Cloud NAT only handles outbound connections from VMs to the internet, not inbound connections to VMs. IAP verifies user identity via IAM before allowing the tunnel.

ul.li: IAP TCP forwarding requires the roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor IAM role on the target VM or project. Without this role, the tunnel request is denied even if the user has compute.instances.get permissions.

A firewall rule must allow TCP ingress from 35.235.240.0/20 (Google's IAP IP range) to the target VM on port 22. This is the only network-level requirement since all traffic routes through Google's backbone.
IAP works for any TCP protocol (SSH, RDP, database connections) by specifying different ports, making it a general-purpose secure access solution. Use --local-host-port for port forwarding.

The alternative approach is a bastion host (jump box) in a public subnet, but this requires managing an additional VM, patching it, and configuring SSH key forwarding. IAP eliminates this operational overhead entirely.

question.title: Deploying to GKE
question.scenario: A DevOps engineer needs to deploy a containerized application to a GKE cluster using kubectl.
question.question-text: After creating a GKE cluster, which command configures kubectl to connect to it?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Is initial cluster authentication setup a kubectl responsibility or a cloud-provider CLI responsibility? Think about which tool owns the credentials.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The command "gcloud container clusters get-credentials CLUSTER_NAME --zone=ZONE" fetches cluster endpoint and authentication details, then writes them to ~/.kube/config. Option A is invalid because kubectl does not have a "connect" subcommand. Option C uses "gcloud kubernetes" which is not a real command group; GKE commands live under "gcloud container". Option D switches between already-configured contexts but cannot set up a new one from scratch. After running get-credentials, kubectl commands automatically target the configured cluster.

ul.li: Use --region instead of --zone for regional clusters (which distribute the control plane across three zones). Using the wrong flag causes a "cluster not found" error that is a common troubleshooting pitfall.
For private clusters with no public endpoint, add --internal-ip to configure kubectl to reach the control plane via the internal network. This requires VPN, Interconnect, or IAP tunnel access.

Workload Identity (--workload-pool=PROJECT.svc.id.goog) is the recommended way for GKE pods to authenticate to GCP APIs. It federates Kubernetes service accounts with IAM service accounts, eliminating the need for exported key files.

Multiple clusters can coexist in ~/.kube/config. Use "kubectl config get-contexts" to list them and "kubectl config use-context CONTEXT" to switch. Each get-credentials call adds or updates a context entry.

question.title: Service Account Management
question.scenario: An application running on Compute Engine needs to access Cloud Storage buckets in a different project.
question.question-text: What is the proper way to grant a VM's service account access to resources in another project?

choices.choice: Create a new service account in the target project
Share the service account key between projects
Use VPC Peering to share access
Grant the service account an IAM role on the target resource in the other project

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: IAM identities are not confined to the project where they were created. What is the simplest way to let an existing identity access a resource it does not currently have permission for?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Grant the VM's service account (e.g., SA_NAME@PROJECT_A.iam.gserviceaccount.com) an IAM role directly on the target resource in PROJECT_B. Option A is unnecessary because service accounts from one project work as valid principals in other projects. Option B is a security anti-pattern since sharing key files creates untracked credentials that cannot be easily revoked. Option D confuses networking (VPC Peering connects networks) with IAM (which controls API-level access). IAM roles can be granted at the project, folder, or individual resource level for fine-grained cross-project access.

ul.li: Always grant the minimum necessary role following the principle of least privilege. For Cloud Storage read access, use roles/storage.objectViewer on the specific bucket rather than a project-wide role like roles/storage.admin.

Service account impersonation (--impersonate-service-account) allows a user or service account to temporarily act as another SA without downloading keys. This is controlled by the roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator role.

Avoid downloading service account JSON keys whenever possible. Prefer attached service accounts on Compute Engine, Workload Identity on GKE, and built-in service account integration on Cloud Run and Cloud Functions.

Use IAM Conditions to add context-based restrictions, such as limiting access to specific time windows or requiring requests to originate from certain IP ranges, adding defense-in-depth beyond basic role grants.

question.title: Choosing Compute Options
question.scenario: A team needs to choose between Compute Engine, GKE, App Engine, and Cloud Run for deploying a stateless web application that experiences variable traffic.
question.question-text: Which compute option provides automatic scaling to zero and per-request billing for a containerized stateless application?

choices.choice: Compute Engine with Managed Instance Groups

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Which of these compute options can run arbitrary containers, charge nothing when idle, and bill per individual request rather than per provisioned resource?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Run is the ideal choice for containerized stateless applications with variable traffic. It automatically scales instances based on concurrent requests (including down to zero when idle), provides per-request billing charged only for CPU and memory consumed during request processing, and requires no infrastructure management. Option A (App Engine Standard) also scales to zero but restricts you to specific language runtimes and does not accept arbitrary container images. Option B (Compute Engine MIGs) requires managing VMs and cannot scale to zero. Option C (GKE Standard) charges for node infrastructure continuously regardless of traffic.

ul.li: Cloud Run's maximum request timeout is 60 minutes (configurable), making it suitable for long-running HTTP operations. Cloud Run jobs handle batch workloads that run to completion without needing an HTTP endpoint.

App Engine Standard supports scale-to-zero but only for supported runtimes (Python, Java, Go, Node.js, PHP, Ruby). App Engine Flexible uses custom containers but does NOT scale to zero, making it a common exam distractor.

Setting --min-instances=1 or higher on Cloud Run prevents cold starts by keeping warm instances ready, trading the cost savings of scale-to-zero for lower latency on the first request after idle periods.

GKE Autopilot charges per pod resource request (not per node), which is closer to serverless pricing than GKE Standard but still does not offer per-request billing or true scale-to-zero at the cluster level.

question.title: Cloud Monitoring Alerting
question.scenario: An operations team needs to be notified when CPU utilization on production VMs exceeds 80% for more than 5 minutes.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Monitoring component is used to define conditions that trigger notifications?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The scenario describes a threshold condition combined with a duration window and a notification action. Only one Monitoring component ties all three of these elements together into a single configuration.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Alerting Policies in Cloud Monitoring combine metric conditions (such as CPU exceeding 80%), duration requirements (such as sustaining that threshold for 5 minutes), and notification channels (email, SMS, PagerDuty, Pub/Sub, webhooks) into a unified alerting configuration. Option A (Dashboards) only visualize metrics and cannot trigger notifications. Option C (Uptime Checks) test endpoint availability but are not general-purpose metric threshold monitors. Option D (Metrics Explorer) is an interactive query tool for ad-hoc investigation, not automated alerting. When the alerting policy conditions are met, an incident is created and notifications are dispatched.

ul.li: Alerting policy conditions support metric thresholds, metric absence (no data received), and rate-of-change triggers. Multi-condition policies combine these with AND/OR logic for complex alerting scenarios.
The documentation field in an alerting policy embeds runbook URLs directly into notifications, giving on-call engineers immediate access to remediation steps when an alert fires.
Notification rate limiting and snooze controls prevent alert storms during widespread outages. Auto-close duration automatically resolves incidents when conditions return to normal.

Log-based alerting policies trigger on specific log entries (e.g., severity=CRITICAL) rather than numeric metrics, enabling alerts on application events, security incidents, or error patterns that are not captured as time-series metrics.

question.title: Cloud Storage Operations
question.scenario: A data engineer needs to copy a large number of files from an on-premises server to a Cloud Storage bucket efficiently.
question.question-text: Which command-line tool and option provides parallel, resumable transfers for Cloud Storage?

choices.choice: gsutil -m cp for parallel operations with automatic resume
bq load for all file transfers

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Which GCP CLI tool is purpose-built for Cloud Storage operations, and how can you enable parallel transfers with it?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The gsutil command with the -m flag enables parallel multi-threaded and multi-process operations for faster bulk transfers. For large files, gsutil automatically switches to resumable uploads (files over 8 MB by default). Use "gsutil -m cp -r SOURCE gs://BUCKET/" for recursive parallel copying. Option A uses a fabricated --fast flag that does not exist. Option C (bq load) is for loading data into BigQuery, not general file transfers. Option D (curl) is low-level and lacks built-in parallelism, resumability, and credential management that gsutil provides out of the box.

ul.li: The newer "gcloud storage" commands (e.g., gcloud storage cp) are the recommended replacement for gsutil. They offer parallel transfers by default and better performance, but gsutil remains widely used and tested on the exam.

gsutil rsync synchronizes a local directory with a Cloud Storage bucket, only transferring changed files. The -d flag deletes destination files not present in the source, making it ideal for maintaining mirrors.

For very large migrations (tens of terabytes or more), Storage Transfer Service or Transfer Appliance (a physical device shipped to Google) are more appropriate than gsutil, which is better suited for routine or moderate-volume transfers.

Composite uploads split large files into components uploaded in parallel, then compose them server-side. The .boto configuration file controls parallel composite upload thresholds, process counts, and thread counts for fine-tuning transfer performance.

question.title: IAM Policy Binding
question.scenario: A project administrator needs to grant the Storage Object Viewer role to a user for a specific bucket only, not the entire project.
question.question-text: Which command grants a role to a user on a specific Cloud Storage bucket?

choices.choice: gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding with bucket filter

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Resource-level IAM bindings use the add-iam-policy-binding subcommand on the specific resource, requiring both a --member and a --role flag to define who gets what access.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The command "gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://BUCKET --member=user:EMAIL --role=roles/storage.objectViewer" grants permissions at the bucket level, following the principle of least privilege. Option A uses an invalid command syntax. Option B applies permissions at the project level (add-iam-policy-binding on the project), which would grant access to all buckets in the project, not just one. Option C uses "gsutil iam set" which overwrites the entire IAM policy rather than adding a single binding. The add-iam-policy-binding pattern is consistent across GCP resources and is the safe way to add permissions without affecting existing bindings.

ul.li: The equivalent legacy command "gsutil iam ch user:EMAIL:objectViewer gs://BUCKET" also modifies bucket IAM, but "gcloud storage buckets" is the modern recommended approach. Know both for the exam since gsutil commands still appear frequently.

Uniform bucket-level access (enabled per bucket) disables legacy ACLs and enforces IAM-only access control. Once enabled for 90 consecutive days it becomes permanent, simplifying audit and compliance.
IAM Conditions allow time-based or attribute-based restrictions on bindings, such as granting access only during business hours or only to objects with a specific prefix (resource.name.startsWith).

Use get-iam-policy to audit current bindings and remove-iam-policy-binding to revoke access. Always prefer additive binding changes over set-iam-policy, which replaces the entire policy and can accidentally remove other bindings.

question.title: Log Analysis
question.scenario: A developer needs to find all error logs from a specific Cloud Run service in the past hour.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Logging query syntax filters logs by resource type, service name, and severity?

choices.choice: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE service="SERVICE" AND level="ERROR"

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Logging has its own query language that uses dot-notation field paths, comparison operators, and logical connectors. It is neither SQL nor a CLI flag-based syntax.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Logging queries use field paths with dot notation (resource.type, resource.labels.service_name), comparison operators (=, !=, >=), and logical operators (AND, OR, NOT). Option A uses CLI flag syntax which does not apply inside the Logs Explorer query box. Option B uses SQL syntax which is valid for BigQuery log analytics but not the standard Logging query language. Option C uses a colon-delimited search syntax that does not exist in Cloud Logging. Severity levels form an ordered enum: DEFAULT, DEBUG, INFO, NOTICE, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL, ALERT, EMERGENCY, so >=ERROR matches ERROR and above.

ul.li: The timestamp field enables time-range filtering (e.g., timestamp>="2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"). In the Logs Explorer UI, the time picker sets this automatically, but in gcloud logging read or API calls you must specify it explicitly.

Log-based metrics extract numeric values from log entries and expose them as Cloud Monitoring time-series, enabling alerting on application-specific patterns like error rates or request counts without custom instrumentation.
Log sinks (configured in the Log Router) export matching logs to Cloud Storage for archival, BigQuery for SQL analysis, or Pub/Sub for real-time streaming to third-party tools like Splunk or Datadog.

For Cloud Run specifically, the resource type is "cloud_run_revision" (not "cloud_run"), and the service name lives under resource.labels.service_name. Getting the resource type wrong is the most common query mistake on the exam.

question.title: Managed Instance Groups
question.scenario: A team needs to deploy a horizontally scalable web application that automatically replaces failed instances and performs rolling updates.
question.question-text: Which resource must be created before creating a Managed Instance Group?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: A Managed Instance Group needs a blueprint that defines exactly how each VM should be configured. Without this blueprint, the MIG cannot create any instances.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Instance templates define the complete VM configuration (machine type, disk image, network, service account, startup script, labels) that a Managed Instance Group uses to create identical VM instances. They are a mandatory prerequisite for MIG creation. Option A (Health Check) enables auto-healing but is not required to create the MIG itself. Option B (Target Pool) is a legacy load balancing concept and is not a MIG dependency. Option D (Load Balancer) distributes traffic to MIG instances but is configured after the MIG exists. Templates are immutable; updating a MIG's configuration requires creating a new template and performing a rolling update.

ul.li: Create templates with "gcloud compute instance-templates create" specifying all desired VM properties. Since templates are immutable, use versioned naming (e.g., web-template-v2) to track configuration changes over time.

Rolling updates (--update-policy=proactive) gradually replace instances with the new template while maintaining availability. Canary updates deploy to a configurable subset first (e.g., --max-surge=1 --max-unavailable=0) for safe progressive rollouts.

Regional MIGs (--region flag) distribute instances across multiple zones within a region, providing automatic zone-level failure resilience. Zonal MIGs are confined to a single zone and do not survive zone outages.

Health checks attached to a MIG enable auto-healing: if an instance fails the health check, the MIG automatically recreates it from the template. Health check configuration (path, port, check interval, unhealthy threshold) directly affects how quickly failures are detected and remediated.

question.title: VPC Network Design
question.scenario: An architect needs to design a network allowing development and production environments to be isolated while sharing some common services.
question.question-text: Which VPC configuration allows multiple projects to use a centrally managed network while maintaining project-level resource isolation?

choices.choice: Single VPC with firewall rules per project
Shared VPC with host and service projects
Multiple standalone VPCs with Cloud VPN

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When you need centralized network administration with decentralized workload ownership, GCP offers a host/service project model that shares subnets without sharing resource management.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Shared VPC designates one host project that owns the VPC network and subnets, while service projects attach to those subnets to deploy resources. This separates network administration (centralized in the host project) from workload management (distributed across service projects). Option B (VPC Peering) connects separate VPCs but creates a mesh of bilateral relationships that becomes complex at scale and does not centralize management. Option C (Cloud VPN) adds encryption overhead and latency for what should be internal traffic. Option D is incorrect because a single VPC cannot span multiple projects; VPCs are project-scoped resources.

ul.li: Shared VPC requires an Organization resource and is configured by a Shared VPC Admin (roles/compute.xpnAdmin) at the organization or folder level. Service projects are attached to specific subnets, not the entire VPC, enabling subnet-level isolation.

Firewall rules in the host project's VPC apply to all service project resources using that network. Network admins control traffic flow centrally while project teams manage their own compute, storage, and application resources.

Cross-project service discovery works natively within a Shared VPC because all attached projects share the same network and DNS. Internal load balancers and private service endpoints are accessible across service project boundaries.

VPC Peering is better suited for connecting independently managed VPCs (e.g., between business units with separate network teams), while Shared VPC is preferred when one team owns the network and multiple teams consume it.

question.title: Snapshots and Backups
question.scenario: A database administrator needs to create point-in-time backups of persistent disks that can be used to restore or create new disks.
question.question-text: Which command creates a snapshot of a Compute Engine persistent disk?

choices.choice: gcloud compute images create from-disk DISK_NAME

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Snapshots are managed as their own resource type under gcloud compute. The create subcommand takes the snapshot name as the primary argument and references the source disk via a flag.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Use "gcloud compute snapshots create SNAPSHOT_NAME --source-disk=DISK_NAME --source-disk-zone=ZONE" to create a point-in-time snapshot. Option B reverses the command structure (snapshots are not a subcommand of disks). Option C uses fabricated command groups. Option D creates a custom image from a disk, which is a different operation used for creating reusable boot disk images rather than backup snapshots. Snapshots are incremental after the first one, meaning only changed blocks are stored, making subsequent snapshots faster and cheaper than full copies.

ul.li: Snapshots are stored in Cloud Storage internally but managed through the Compute Engine API. They can create new disks in any zone or region, enabling cross-region disaster recovery and migration scenarios.
Snapshot schedules (resource policies) automate recurring snapshots by attaching a schedule to a disk. Configure retention policies to automatically delete old snapshots and control storage costs.

For database disks, use the --guest-flush flag (Windows) or freeze the filesystem before snapshotting (Linux) to ensure application-consistent snapshots. Without this, the snapshot captures a crash-consistent state that may require database recovery on restore.

Images (gcloud compute images create) are better for creating reusable boot disk templates, while snapshots are optimized for backup and restore workflows. Images can be shared across projects and used in instance templates; snapshots are typically project-scoped.

question.title: API Enablement
question.scenario: A developer receives a "API not enabled" error when trying to create a Cloud SQL instance in a new project.
question.question-text: Which command enables an API for a GCP project?

choices.choice: gcloud config set api sql enabled

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: API management in GCP uses the gcloud services command group. APIs are identified by their full googleapis.com domain name, not by shorthand abbreviations.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Use "gcloud services enable API_NAME" to enable an API for the current project. API names follow the pattern service.googleapis.com (e.g., sqladmin.googleapis.com for Cloud SQL, compute.googleapis.com for Compute Engine). Option B uses a nonexistent "gcloud api" command group and a shorthand name. Option C misuses gcloud config, which manages SDK settings not project APIs. Option D invents a "gcloud projects enable-api" command that does not exist. Use "gcloud services list --available" to discover available APIs and "gcloud services list --enabled" to see what is already active.

ul.li: APIs must be enabled per project. A new project starts with almost all APIs disabled. Enabling an API may automatically enable its dependencies (e.g., enabling the GKE API also enables the Compute Engine API).

Organization policies (constraints/serviceuser.services) can restrict which APIs can be enabled across projects, preventing teams from using unapproved services. This is a key governance control for enterprise environments.

Disabling an API with "gcloud services disable" prevents new operations but does not delete existing resources. Re-enabling the API restores access to those resources. However, some APIs have dependencies that prevent disabling if other enabled APIs rely on them.

You can enable multiple APIs in a single command: "gcloud services enable sqladmin.googleapis.com compute.googleapis.com storage.googleapis.com". This is faster than enabling them one at a time since each enable call has API overhead.

question.title: App Engine Deployment
question.scenario: A developer needs to deploy a Python Flask application to App Engine Standard environment.
question.question-text: Which file is required for App Engine deployment and specifies runtime configuration?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: App Engine requires a YAML configuration file in the application root that declares the runtime, scaling behavior, URL handlers, and environment settings for deployment.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: app.yaml is the mandatory configuration file for App Engine deployment, specifying the runtime (e.g., python39, nodejs18), URL handlers, scaling settings, environment variables, and resource limits. Option B (config.py) is an application-level configuration file with no special meaning to App Engine. Option C (requirements.txt) lists Python dependencies but is not the deployment configuration; it is consumed during the build step. Option D (Dockerfile) is used by App Engine Flexible environment for custom runtimes, but is not required for Standard environment and does not replace app.yaml. Deploy with "gcloud app deploy" from the directory containing app.yaml.

ul.li: App Engine supports multiple services within a single application. The "service:" field in app.yaml names the service; omitting it deploys to the "default" service. Each service can have its own runtime, scaling, and configuration.

dispatch.yaml routes incoming requests to specific services based on URL patterns, enabling microservice architectures. cron.yaml defines scheduled tasks, and queue.yaml configures task queues for background processing.

App Engine Standard has two scaling types: automatic (scales based on traffic, including to zero) and basic/manual. The scaling configuration in app.yaml controls instance count, idle timeout, and concurrent request limits.

App Engine Flexible environment supports custom Docker containers and runs on Compute Engine VMs behind the scenes. It does NOT scale to zero (minimum one instance always running), which is a critical distinction from Standard on the exam.

question.title: Cloud SQL Administration
question.scenario: A DBA needs to create a read replica of a Cloud SQL PostgreSQL instance in a different zone for high availability.
question.question-text: Which gcloud command creates a read replica of a Cloud SQL instance?

choices.choice: gcloud sql instances clone PRIMARY_NAME REPLICA_NAME
gcloud sql instances replicate PRIMARY_NAME to REPLICA_NAME

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Read replicas are created using the standard instances create command with a flag that designates the primary instance. There is no separate "replicas" subcommand group in gcloud sql.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Create a read replica with "gcloud sql instances create REPLICA_NAME --master-instance-name=PRIMARY_NAME". The --zone flag places the replica in a different zone for resilience. Option A (clone) creates an independent copy of the database that does not receive ongoing replication from the source. Option B uses a "replicas" command group that does not exist in gcloud sql. Option D uses a fabricated "replicate" verb. Replicas asynchronously replicate data from the primary and serve read-only queries, reducing load on the primary instance for read-heavy workloads.

ul.li: Cloud SQL high availability (HA) is configured separately from read replicas using --availability-type=REGIONAL on the primary instance. HA provides automatic failover to a standby in another zone, while read replicas are for scaling read traffic and do not automatically become the primary.

Read replicas can be promoted to standalone instances with "gcloud sql instances promote-replica", which permanently breaks replication. This is useful for blue-green deployments or migrating workloads to a new primary.

Cross-region replicas enable geographic read distribution and disaster recovery but incur network egress charges for replication traffic between regions. Replication lag increases with geographic distance.

The clone command (Option A) creates a point-in-time independent copy using binary log coordinates, which is useful for creating test environments or one-time database copies, not for ongoing replication.

question.title: Custom Roles
question.scenario: A security team needs to create a role that has specific permissions not available in any predefined role combination.
question.question-text: Which command creates a custom IAM role at the project level?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Custom roles are managed under the gcloud iam roles command group. The create subcommand requires a role ID, project scope, and a comma-separated list of granular permissions.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Create custom roles with "gcloud iam roles create ROLE_ID --project=PROJECT --permissions=permission1,permission2 --title='Display Name' --description='Description'". Option B misuses "add-role" which is not a valid command (add-iam-policy-binding grants existing roles to members). Option C confuses policies with roles; IAM policies are bindings of roles to members, not role definitions. Option D uses "gcloud roles" which is not a real command group; the correct path is "gcloud iam roles". Alternatively, use --file to specify a YAML definition containing the permissions list, title, description, and launch stage.

ul.li: Custom roles can be created at the organization level (--organization=ORG_ID) or project level (--project=PROJECT_ID). Organization-level roles can be granted on any resource within the org, while project-level roles are scoped to that project only.

The --stage flag sets the role's lifecycle phase: ALPHA, BETA, GA, DEPRECATED, or DISABLED. Use DISABLED to temporarily revoke all grants of the role without deleting it, and DEPRECATED to signal that a replacement role should be used.

Use "gcloud iam list-testable-permissions RESOURCE" to discover which permissions are available for a given resource type. Custom roles cannot include permissions that are not yet testable or are restricted to predefined roles only.

There is a limit of 300 custom roles per organization and 300 per project. Custom roles can contain up to 3000 permissions. Plan custom role strategy carefully to avoid hitting these limits in large enterprises.

question.title: Load Balancer Configuration
question.scenario: A team needs to set up an HTTPS load balancer to distribute traffic across multiple regions with a single global IP address.
question.question-text: Which type of load balancer provides a single global anycast IP and handles SSL termination?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Only one GCP load balancer type provides a single anycast IP address that routes users to the nearest healthy backend across all regions. The key words are "global" and "SSL termination."

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Global external Application Load Balancer (formerly called HTTP(S) Load Balancer) provides a single anycast IP address that automatically routes users to the closest healthy backend region. It terminates SSL/TLS at the edge, handles URL-based routing via URL maps, and integrates with Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor. Option B is regional only and operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), so it cannot perform SSL termination or content-based routing. Option C is for internal traffic between VMs and has no public-facing endpoint. Option D is regional and internal, suitable for microservice-to-microservice traffic within a single region, not global public traffic.

ul.li: The Global Application Load Balancer is assembled from multiple components: a global forwarding rule (binds the IP and port), a target HTTPS proxy (handles SSL certificates), a URL map (routes requests to backend services), and backend services (point to instance groups or NEGs).

Google-managed SSL certificates automatically provision and renew TLS certificates for your domains at no additional cost. Self-managed certificates can also be uploaded for domains requiring specific certificate configurations.

Cloud CDN can be enabled on backend services to cache static content at Google's global edge locations, reducing latency and backend load. Cache invalidation is available for immediate content updates.

Cloud Armor integrates with the load balancer to provide DDoS protection, IP allowlisting/denylisting, rate limiting, and WAF rules (OWASP Top 10) at the edge, blocking malicious traffic before it reaches your backends.

question.title: Quota Management
question.scenario: A team receives an error indicating they've reached the maximum number of CPUs for their project in a specific region.
question.question-text: How can a team request an increase to their project's compute quota?

choices.choice: Edit the quota value directly in gcloud
Submit a quota increase request through the Cloud Console Quotas page
Create a new project with higher default quotas
Quotas cannot be increased after project creation

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Quotas are enforced limits that require a formal request process to increase. They cannot be self-service edited through the CLI or reset by creating new projects.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Request quota increases through the IAM & Admin > Quotas page in Cloud Console. Select the specific quota, click Edit Quotas, specify the desired new limit, and provide a justification. Google reviews requests and may approve, partially approve, or deny based on your billing account history and regional capacity. Option A is incorrect because quotas cannot be directly edited via gcloud. Option B is wrong because new projects receive the same default quotas. Option D is incorrect because quotas are adjustable through the request process, and some quotas increase automatically as your usage history grows.

ul.li: GCP has two types of quotas: rate quotas (requests per time period, e.g., API calls per minute) that reset automatically, and allocation quotas (resource limits, e.g., maximum CPUs per region) that remain until changed. The exam tests whether you know the difference.
Billing account standing and payment history significantly affect quota approval speed and likelihood. New accounts with no spending history may face lower initial quotas and slower approval times.

Use "gcloud compute project-info describe --project=PROJECT" to view current compute quotas and usage. The "gcloud compute regions describe REGION" command shows region-specific quota limits and current consumption.

Organization quota policies allow administrators to set upper bounds on quotas across all projects, preventing any single project from consuming a disproportionate share of organizational resources. This is essential for multi-team environments with shared billing.

question.title: Cloud Run Deployment
question.scenario: A developer wants to deploy a container image from Artifact Registry to Cloud Run with environment variables and minimum instances.
question.question-text: Which command deploys a container to Cloud Run with configuration options?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Run services are managed under the gcloud run command group. The deploy subcommand handles both creating new services and updating existing ones with a single command.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Deploy to Cloud Run with "gcloud run deploy SERVICE --image=IMAGE --region=REGION". The --set-env-vars flag configures environment variables, --min-instances prevents cold starts by keeping warm instances, and --max-instances caps scaling. Option A uses kubectl which is for Kubernetes clusters, not managed Cloud Run. Option B uses "gcloud container run" which is not a valid command group; Cloud Run commands are under "gcloud run". Option C uses --container instead of --image and uses "services create" instead of the simpler "deploy" which handles both create and update operations. Additional flags include --memory, --cpu, and --allow-unauthenticated for public access.

ul.li: The --service-account flag specifies the runtime identity for the Cloud Run service, controlling which GCP APIs and resources it can access. Always use a dedicated service account with minimal permissions rather than the default compute service account.

The --vpc-connector flag attaches a Serverless VPC Access connector, enabling the Cloud Run service to reach private resources like Cloud SQL private IPs, Memorystore instances, or internal VMs without exposing them publicly.

The --ingress flag controls who can reach the service: "all" (public internet), "internal" (only from VPC and other GCP services), or "internal-and-cloud-load-balancing" (internal plus global load balancer). This is a critical security setting for production services.

The --source flag builds directly from source code (using Cloud Build and Buildpacks) instead of requiring a pre-built container image. This simplifies deployment for applications that do not need custom Dockerfiles.

question.title: VPC Firewall Rules
question.scenario: An administrator needs to allow HTTPS traffic from the internet to VMs with the "web-server" network tag.
question.question-text: Which command creates a firewall rule allowing HTTPS ingress to tagged instances?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: VPC firewall rules are managed under gcloud compute firewall-rules. The command specifies what traffic to allow, which instances are targeted (by network tag), and where traffic originates from.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The correct command is "gcloud compute firewall-rules create RULE_NAME --allow=PROTOCOL:PORT --target-tags=TAG --source-ranges=IP_RANGE". The --allow flag specifies protocol and port (tcp:443 for HTTPS), --target-tags selects which VMs the rule applies to, and --source-ranges=0.0.0.0/0 allows traffic from any IP. Options B, C, and D all use incorrect command groups (there is no "gcloud vpc", "gcloud network rules", or "gcloud firewall"). The --direction flag defaults to INGRESS. For service-account-based targeting instead of network tags, use --target-service-accounts, which is more secure because tags can be added by anyone with instance edit permissions.

ul.li: Firewall rule priority ranges from 0 (highest) to 65535 (lowest), with a default of 1000. GCP evaluates rules from highest to lowest priority, and the first matching rule determines whether traffic is allowed or denied. This means a deny rule at priority 900 overrides an allow rule at 1000.

Every VPC has two implied rules at the lowest priority (65535): deny all ingress and allow all egress. These cannot be deleted but can be overridden by higher-priority explicit rules. The default network also has pre-created allow rules for internal traffic and common protocols.

Firewall Rules Logging (--enable-logging) records metadata about every connection that matches the rule, including source/destination IPs, ports, protocol, and whether traffic was allowed or denied. This is essential for security auditing and troubleshooting connectivity issues.

Hierarchical firewall policies (at the organization or folder level) take precedence over VPC-level firewall rules, allowing centralized security teams to enforce baseline rules (e.g., deny known malicious IP ranges) that individual projects cannot override.

question.title: Debugging with Serial Console
question.scenario: A VM is unresponsive to SSH and an administrator needs to access it for troubleshooting.
question.question-text: What must be configured to enable interactive serial console access to a Compute Engine VM?

choices.choice: Serial console is always available without configuration
Request serial console access from GCP support
Enable serial-port-enable metadata on the VM or project, and use gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port
Install serial console agent on the VM

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Interactive serial console access is disabled by default for security reasons. It must be explicitly enabled through instance or project metadata before the connection command will work.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Enable interactive serial console access by setting the metadata key "serial-port-enable" to "TRUE" on the instance or project. Then connect with "gcloud compute connect-to-serial-port INSTANCE_NAME". Option A is wrong because serial console access is disabled by default as a security measure. Option C is incorrect because serial console access is a hypervisor-level feature that requires no in-guest agent installation. Option D is wrong because this is a self-service configuration, not a support request. Serial console provides direct console access even when SSH, networking, and the OS are completely non-functional, making it invaluable for boot failures and kernel panics.

ul.li: Serial console access requires the roles/compute.instanceAdmin.v1 IAM role or specifically the compute.instances.getSerialPortOutput permission. The user must also have compute.instances.setMetadata if enabling the metadata themselves.

Organization policies can block serial console access entirely using the constraints/compute.disableSerialPortAccess constraint. When this policy is active, setting the metadata key has no effect, which is a common troubleshooting scenario on the exam.

Port 1 provides the interactive console; ports 2-4 provide read-only output that captures boot messages, kernel logs, and startup script output. Use "gcloud compute instances get-serial-port-output" to read historical serial output without an interactive session.

For Shielded VMs, serial console access may be restricted by secure boot settings. Additionally, the serial console connection authenticates through Google's infrastructure, so it works even when the VM's network interface is misconfigured or the firewall blocks all traffic.

question.title: Cloud Functions Deployment
question.scenario: A developer needs to deploy a Python function triggered by Cloud Pub/Sub messages.
question.question-text: Which command deploys a Pub/Sub-triggered Cloud Function?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Functions uses the gcloud functions command group. Event triggers are specified with --trigger-topic for Pub/Sub, and the runtime flag declares which language version to execute.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Deploy a Pub/Sub-triggered Cloud Function with "gcloud functions deploy FUNCTION_NAME --runtime=python39 --trigger-topic=TOPIC_NAME --entry-point=FUNCTION". The --entry-point specifies which function in your code handles the event. Option B incorrectly nests functions under the pubsub command group. Option C conflates Cloud Run with Cloud Functions; while related, they use different deployment commands. Option D uses a fabricated "gcloud deploy" command. Cloud Functions receive Pub/Sub messages as base64-encoded data in the event payload, which must be decoded in the function code before processing.

ul.li: Cloud Functions 2nd gen (deployed with --gen2 flag) runs on Cloud Run infrastructure and uses Eventarc for event routing. It supports larger instances (up to 16 GB RAM, 4 vCPUs), longer timeouts (up to 60 minutes), concurrency (multiple requests per instance), and traffic splitting for gradual rollouts.

Other trigger types include --trigger-http for HTTP endpoints, --trigger-bucket for Cloud Storage events (object create, delete, archive, metadata update), and --trigger-event-filters for Eventarc-based triggers in 2nd gen functions.

The --source flag specifies the function code location: a local directory (default: current directory), a Cloud Source Repository, or a Cloud Storage archive. The --env-vars-file flag loads environment variables from a YAML file for configuration management.

Cold starts occur when a new function instance must be initialized. Minimize cold start latency by keeping dependencies lightweight, using --min-instances to keep warm instances, and avoiding heavy initialization in the global scope of your function code.

question.title: Database Selection
question.scenario: A company needs to choose a database for their globally distributed application that requires strong consistency, relational queries, and horizontal scaling.
question.question-text: Which GCP database provides relational semantics with global distribution and strong consistency?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Only one GCP database simultaneously offers relational schemas with SQL, horizontal scaling across regions, and externally consistent transactions. The other options each lack at least one of these requirements.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Spanner is GCP's globally distributed relational database that uniquely combines SQL queries, ACID transactions, relational schemas, and horizontal scaling with strong (external) consistency. It uses Google's TrueTime API with atomic clocks to synchronize data across regions. Option B (Cloud SQL) is a managed relational database (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server) but cannot scale horizontally or distribute globally. Option C (Firestore) is a NoSQL document database without relational joins or SQL support. Option D (Cloud Bigtable) is a NoSQL wide-column store optimized for high throughput but lacks relational features and SQL query support.

ul.li: Cloud Spanner offers a 99.999% (five nines) availability SLA for multi-region configurations and 99.99% for regional configurations. This is the highest SLA of any GCP database product and a frequent exam topic.

Spanner supports both Google Standard SQL and PostgreSQL interface dialects. The PostgreSQL interface enables existing PostgreSQL applications to migrate with minimal code changes while gaining Spanner's horizontal scalability.

Spanner's minimum cost is one processing unit (approximately $0.90/hour for regional), making it expensive for small workloads. For applications that need relational SQL without global distribution, Cloud SQL is typically more cost-effective.

Interleaved tables physically co-locate parent and child rows for optimal join performance. Change streams enable real-time CDC (Change Data Capture) for replicating Spanner data to BigQuery, Pub/Sub, or external systems.

question.title: Instance Metadata
question.scenario: A startup script needs to retrieve the project ID and instance zone at runtime from within a Compute Engine VM.
question.question-text: How does a VM access its own metadata including project ID and zone?

choices.choice: Access environment variables set by Compute Engine

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Compute Engine exposes instance and project metadata through a special HTTP endpoint accessible only from within the VM. Requests require a specific header for authentication.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: VMs query the metadata server at http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/ with the required header "Metadata-Flavor: Google". This provides paths like /project/project-id, /instance/zone, and /instance/service-accounts/default/token for access tokens. Option A is incorrect because there is no /etc/gcp/metadata file on GCP VMs. Option C would work but requires the gcloud SDK to be installed and authenticated, adding unnecessary dependency. Option D is wrong because Compute Engine does not set environment variables with metadata; the metadata server is the designated mechanism. The metadata server enables dynamic configuration without hardcoding project-specific values.

ul.li: Service account access tokens are obtained from the metadata server at /instance/service-accounts/default/token. Client libraries (e.g., google-cloud-python) automatically use this mechanism when running on GCP, enabling credential-free authentication in application code.

Custom metadata set at instance or project level is accessible under /instance/attributes/KEY and /project/attributes/KEY respectively. This is the recommended way to pass configuration (database URLs, feature flags) to VMs without baking them into images.

The wait-for-change endpoint (appending ?wait_for_change=true&last_etag=ETAG) enables long-polling for metadata updates. Scripts can watch for configuration changes in real time without periodic polling, enabling dynamic reconfiguration of running applications.

The metadata server is accessible only from within the VM instance at the link-local address 169.254.169.254 (also reachable via metadata.google.internal). It cannot be reached from outside the VM, providing a security boundary for sensitive data like service account tokens.

question.title: OS Login
question.scenario: An organization wants to manage SSH access to VMs using corporate identities and two-factor authentication.
question.question-text: Which feature enables SSH key and user account management using Cloud Identity?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP offers a feature that links Linux user accounts directly to Cloud Identity or Google Workspace accounts, replacing manual SSH key management with IAM-based access control.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: OS Login manages SSH access using IAM roles instead of manually distributed SSH keys in project or instance metadata. Users' SSH public keys are associated with their Google/Cloud Identity accounts, and access is controlled by IAM roles: roles/compute.osLogin for standard access and roles/compute.osAdminLogin for sudo access. Option B (Project-wide SSH keys) stores keys in project metadata but does not integrate with Cloud Identity or support 2FA. Option C (IAP TCP Forwarding) provides network-level tunneling for SSH but does not manage user accounts or SSH keys on the VMs. Option D (Serial Console) is for emergency debugging, not identity-based access management.

ul.li: Enable OS Login by setting the metadata key "enable-oslogin" to "TRUE" at the project or instance level. Once enabled, SSH keys in project metadata are ignored, and all access is managed through IAM roles and Cloud Identity accounts.

OS Login automatically creates and manages POSIX user accounts on VMs, mapping Cloud Identity users to consistent UIDs/GIDs across all instances. This eliminates UID conflicts and simplifies file permission management in shared environments.

Two-factor authentication is enabled with "enable-oslogin-2fa" metadata set to "TRUE". Users must complete a 2FA challenge (security key, phone prompt, or TOTP code) in addition to SSH key authentication before gaining access.

Organization policies can enforce OS Login across all projects (constraints/compute.requireOsLogin), ensuring that no project can fall back to legacy SSH key management. This is a key security hardening recommendation for enterprise GCP deployments.

question.title: GKE Workload Deployment
question.scenario: A team needs to deploy a stateless application to GKE with 3 replicas and expose it externally.
question.question-text: Which kubectl commands create a deployment with replicas and expose it with an external load balancer?

choices.choice: kubectl create deployment NAME --image=IMAGE --replicas=3, then kubectl expose deployment NAME --type=LoadBalancer --port=80

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Creating a deployment and exposing it are two separate kubectl operations. The deployment manages the pods, while the service (created by expose) provides network access to them.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: First create a deployment with "kubectl create deployment NAME --image=IMAGE --replicas=3", then expose it with "kubectl expose deployment NAME --type=LoadBalancer --port=80 --target-port=8080". On GKE, the LoadBalancer type automatically provisions a GCP Network Load Balancer with an external IP. Option B uses deprecated kubectl run flags; --replicas and --expose are no longer supported for creating deployments. Option C uses "kubectl deploy" which is not a valid command. Option D uses gcloud for Kubernetes workload management, but GKE workloads are managed through kubectl, not gcloud container commands.

ul.li: Declarative management with "kubectl apply -f" and YAML manifests is the production-recommended approach over imperative commands. YAML files can be version-controlled, reviewed, and applied consistently across environments, enabling GitOps workflows.

Service types determine network exposure: ClusterIP (internal only, default), NodePort (exposes on each node's IP at a static port 30000-32767), and LoadBalancer (provisions a cloud load balancer with an external IP). Ingress resources provide more sophisticated HTTP routing with path-based and host-based rules.

Use "kubectl scale deployment NAME --replicas=N" to adjust replica count after creation. Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) automates this based on CPU, memory, or custom metrics, while Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) adjusts resource requests and limits.

On GKE, annotations on the Service resource control load balancer behavior. For example, cloud.google.com/neg enables container-native load balancing via Network Endpoint Groups, routing traffic directly to pods instead of through node-level iptables for better performance.

question.title: Export Logs
question.scenario: A security team needs to retain all audit logs for 7 years in compliance with regulations.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Logging feature exports logs to Cloud Storage, BigQuery, or Pub/Sub for long-term retention?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The Log Router is the central component that routes incoming log entries to destinations. Sinks are the configuration objects within the router that define where matching logs should be exported.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Log sinks, configured in the Log Router, export matching log entries to external destinations: Cloud Storage (cost-effective archival for compliance), BigQuery (SQL-based log analytics), Pub/Sub (real-time streaming to third-party SIEM tools), or other Cloud Logging buckets. Option A (Log Buckets) are storage containers within Cloud Logging with configurable retention (up to 10 years) but are not the export mechanism itself. Option B (Log Metrics) extract numeric values from logs for monitoring dashboards, not for log export. Option D (Log Alerting) triggers notifications based on log content but does not export or retain logs. Sinks use inclusion filters to select which logs to route, and multiple sinks can export the same logs to different destinations simultaneously.

ul.li: Exclusion filters in the Log Router prevent matching logs from being stored in Cloud Logging at all, reducing storage costs. This is commonly used to exclude verbose debug logs or high-volume load balancer health check logs that provide little value.

Aggregated sinks can be created at the organization or folder level to export logs from all child projects to a central destination, enabling enterprise-wide security monitoring and compliance without configuring sinks in every individual project.

The sink's writer identity (a service account) must have write permissions on the destination resource. For cross-project sinks, you must explicitly grant the sink's service account access to the destination bucket, BigQuery dataset, or Pub/Sub topic.

Cloud Logging has two default sinks: _Required (audit logs, retained 400 days, cannot be modified) and _Default (all other logs, retained 30 days, can be disabled). Neither can be deleted, but _Default can have exclusion filters added to reduce ingestion costs.

question.title: Cloud Storage ACLs vs IAM
question.scenario: An administrator is deciding between using ACLs and IAM for Cloud Storage bucket permissions.
question.question-text: What is the recommended access control method for Cloud Storage that simplifies permission management?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Google recommends a bucket-level setting that disables legacy object-level ACLs entirely, consolidating all access control through the standard IAM system used across all GCP services.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Uniform bucket-level access disables ACLs and enforces IAM as the sole access control mechanism for the bucket and its objects. This simplifies permission management, makes access auditable through IAM policy analysis tools, and enables organization-wide policies. Option A (public access) is a severe security risk for most data. Option B (fine-grained ACLs) provides per-object control but creates a complex, hard-to-audit permission model where IAM and ACLs can conflict. Option C (Signed URLs) provides temporary, time-limited access to specific objects and is appropriate for sharing individual files, not for managing ongoing bucket permissions.

ul.li: Once uniform bucket-level access has been enabled continuously for 90 days, it becomes permanently locked on and cannot be reverted to fine-grained ACL mode. Plan this transition carefully, as there is no undo after the 90-day window.

The domain-restricted sharing organization policy (constraints/iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains) requires uniform bucket-level access to function correctly. Buckets with ACLs enabled can bypass domain restrictions through legacy ACL grants.

IAM Conditions work only with uniform bucket-level access, enabling rules like "grant read access only to objects with prefix 'public/'" or "allow access only during business hours." These conditions are not available when ACLs are active.

Signed URLs and signed policy documents work independently of whether uniform access or ACLs are enabled. They are the recommended mechanism for granting temporary access to external users who do not have Google accounts or IAM roles.

question.title: High Availability Design
question.scenario: An architect needs to design a web application that remains available even if an entire zone fails.
question.question-text: Which approach provides zone-level failure resilience for Compute Engine workloads?

choices.choice: Single VM with multiple network interfaces
Regional Managed Instance Group with instances across multiple zones
Zonal MIG with higher replica count

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Surviving a zone failure requires instances distributed across multiple zones. Only one MIG configuration automatically manages this multi-zone distribution as a single scalable unit.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Regional Managed Instance Groups distribute VM instances across multiple zones within a region automatically. If one zone experiences an outage, instances in the remaining zones continue serving traffic and the MIG can recreate lost instances in healthy zones. Option A (zonal MIG) places all instances in a single zone, so a zone failure takes down all of them regardless of replica count. Option B (multiple network interfaces) improves network redundancy within a single VM but does not address zone-level failure. Option D (preemptible VMs) can be terminated by Google at any time with 30 seconds notice and provide no availability guarantees, making them unsuitable for high-availability designs.

ul.li: Regional MIGs use proactive redistribution by default, which maintains an even distribution of instances across zones. If a zone becomes unhealthy, the MIG automatically redistributes instances to the remaining zones to maintain the target size.

For multi-region resilience (surviving an entire region outage), deploy separate regional MIGs in multiple regions behind a Global Application Load Balancer. The load balancer routes traffic to the nearest healthy region automatically.

Regional persistent disks replicate data synchronously across two zones within a region, providing disk-level resilience that complements regional MIGs. They enable stateful workloads to survive zone failures without data loss.

Update policies on regional MIGs control rolling update behavior: --max-surge (extra instances during update), --max-unavailable (instances that can be offline), and --replacement-method (recreate vs. substitute) determine the tradeoff between update speed and availability during deployments.

question.title: VM Maintenance
question.scenario: A production VM is scheduled for host maintenance and the application cannot tolerate restarts.
question.question-text: What Compute Engine feature allows VMs to continue running during infrastructure maintenance?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Google transparently moves running VMs between physical hosts during maintenance events. This is the default behavior for most VM types and requires no action from the user.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Live migration transparently moves a running VM from one physical host to another during maintenance events without interrupting the guest operating system. The VM's memory, storage, and network state are transferred with only a brief sub-second pause during the final switchover. Option A (custom machine types) controls resource allocation, not maintenance behavior. Option C (sole-tenant nodes) provides hardware isolation but still uses live migration for maintenance. Option D (preemptible mode) always terminates VMs during maintenance events with no migration option, making it the opposite of what is needed for applications that cannot tolerate restarts.

ul.li: The onHostMaintenance setting has two options: MIGRATE (live migration, the default) and TERMINATE. Some workloads (especially those using GPUs or local SSDs) cannot be live-migrated and must be set to TERMINATE because the hardware state cannot be transferred between hosts.

Preemptible and Spot VMs always terminate during maintenance events and cannot use live migration. They also have a maximum lifetime of 24 hours and can be preempted at any time when Google needs the capacity back.

Maintenance event notifications can be received via the metadata server (scheduling/maintenanceEvent endpoint) and Pub/Sub, giving applications advance warning to gracefully drain connections or checkpoint state before the migration pause.

Simulated maintenance events (gcloud compute instances simulate-maintenance-event) allow testing how an application handles the brief pause during live migration, helping validate that connection timeouts, health checks, and retry logic are configured correctly.

question.title: Container Image Management
question.scenario: A team wants to automatically scan container images for vulnerabilities before deploying to GKE.
question.question-text: Which Artifact Registry feature automatically identifies security vulnerabilities in container images?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Artifact Registry includes an automated feature that analyzes pushed container images against known vulnerability databases and reports CVEs with severity ratings.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Artifact Registry's vulnerability scanning automatically analyzes container images for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) when they are pushed to the registry and continuously as new vulnerabilities are discovered. Option A (Container Analysis API) is the underlying API and storage layer that powers vulnerability scanning, but it is not the user-facing feature name. Option B (Binary Authorization) is a separate service that enforces deployment policies by requiring attestations before images can be deployed to GKE, but it does not perform scanning itself. Option D (Image signing) creates cryptographic attestations to verify image integrity but does not identify vulnerabilities. Scan results include severity ratings (Critical, High, Medium, Low), CVE identifiers, affected packages, and fix versions.

ul.li: Vulnerability scanning requires enabling the Container Scanning API (containerscanning.googleapis.com) on the project. Without this API enabled, images are stored but not scanned, which is a common oversight in new projects.

Binary Authorization and vulnerability scanning work together in a defense-in-depth approach: scanning identifies vulnerabilities, and Binary Authorization can enforce policies that block deployment of images with Critical or High severity findings until they are remediated.

On-demand scanning (gcloud artifacts docker images scan) analyzes images stored anywhere, not just in Artifact Registry. This is useful for scanning images in CI/CD pipelines before they are pushed to the registry.

Pub/Sub notifications (via the Container Analysis API) can trigger automated responses when new vulnerabilities are found in already-deployed images, enabling workflows that automatically roll back or patch affected deployments.

question.title: Workload Identity
question.scenario: A GKE pod needs to access Cloud Storage without using service account keys.
question.question-text: Which GKE feature allows pods to authenticate as GCP service accounts without key files?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GKE provides a federation mechanism that maps Kubernetes service accounts to GCP IAM service accounts, allowing pods to authenticate to GCP APIs without any exported key files.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Workload Identity federates Kubernetes service accounts with GCP IAM service accounts, enabling pods to authenticate to GCP APIs as the linked IAM service account without downloading or storing key files. Option A (Kubernetes Service Account) provides identity within the cluster but cannot authenticate to GCP APIs by itself. Option B (Node service account) is the service account attached to the underlying GKE node VM; using it gives all pods on the node the same broad permissions, violating least privilege. Option D (Secret Manager) stores secrets securely but would still require managing and rotating service account keys, which Workload Identity eliminates entirely.

ul.li: Enable Workload Identity on the cluster with --workload-pool=PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog during creation or update. This configures the GKE metadata server to intercept token requests from pods and return federated tokens instead of the node's service account token.

The setup requires three steps: (1) annotate the Kubernetes SA with iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=GSA_EMAIL, (2) bind the IAM SA to the K8s SA with roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser, and (3) configure pods to use the annotated Kubernetes SA.

Workload Identity eliminates the need to create, distribute, and rotate service account JSON key files, which are the most common source of credential leaks in GCP environments. Google's security best practices strongly recommend Workload Identity for all GKE workloads.

Each Kubernetes namespace/service-account pair maps to exactly one IAM service account, enabling fine-grained per-workload IAM permissions. Different pods in different namespaces can have different GCP permissions without sharing a single over-privileged node service account.

question.title: Uptime Checks
question.scenario: A team needs to monitor their public website's availability and receive alerts if it goes down.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Monitoring feature tests URL endpoints for availability from multiple global locations?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Monitoring has a dedicated feature that probes HTTP, HTTPS, or TCP endpoints from Google-operated locations worldwide, verifying that your service responds correctly from an external perspective.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Uptime Checks in Cloud Monitoring probe endpoints from multiple geographic locations at configurable intervals, verifying HTTP status codes, response content, and latency. Combined with alerting policies, they notify teams when services become unavailable. Option A (Trace spans) measure request latency through distributed services, not endpoint availability. Option B (Alerting Policies) define notification conditions but do not perform the actual endpoint probing. Option C (Health Checks) are used by load balancers to assess backend instance health internally and cannot test external-facing URLs from the public internet. The distinction between Health Checks (infrastructure) and Uptime Checks (monitoring) is a frequent exam topic.

ul.li: Uptime checks test external endpoint availability from Google's perspective. Health checks test internal backend instance health for load balancer routing decisions. Understanding this distinction is critical because the exam frequently presents scenarios that test which one to use.

Check intervals range from 1 to 15 minutes, and checks run from up to six global regions. A check is considered failed only when multiple regions report failure simultaneously, reducing false positives from transient network issues.
Content matching validates that the response body contains (or does not contain) expected text, catching situations where a server returns HTTP 200 but serves an error page or cached stale content.

Private uptime checks can test internal resources (VMs with only internal IPs, internal load balancers) by routing probe traffic through a VPC network. This requires configuring a Service Directory service to define the internal endpoint for the uptime check.

question.title: Cloud Pub/Sub
question.scenario: A development team needs to set up asynchronous communication between microservices with guaranteed message delivery.
question.question-text: Which Pub/Sub components are required for a subscriber to receive messages?

choices.choice: Only a Topic with subscriber email

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Pub/Sub decouples publishers from subscribers using two distinct resource types. Publishers send to one resource, and each subscriber receives from a separate resource attached to it.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Publishers send messages to a topic, and subscribers receive messages through a subscription attached to that topic. Both resources are required for end-to-end message delivery. Option A uses terminology from other messaging systems (channels/listeners) not applicable to Pub/Sub. Option B is incorrect because a topic alone cannot deliver messages; a subscription resource must be created explicitly. Option C uses queue/consumer terminology from systems like RabbitMQ or SQS, not Pub/Sub. Multiple subscriptions can attach to one topic, and each subscription independently receives all messages published to the topic, enabling fan-out patterns where different services process the same events differently.

ul.li: Pull subscriptions require the subscriber to poll for messages (suitable for batch processing or when the subscriber controls the pace). Push subscriptions deliver messages to an HTTPS endpoint automatically (suitable for Cloud Run, Cloud Functions, or webhook-based integrations).

Messages remain in a subscription until explicitly acknowledged by the subscriber. The acknowledgment deadline (configurable, default 10 seconds) determines how long Pub/Sub waits before redelivering an unacknowledged message, enabling at-least-once delivery guarantees.

Dead-letter topics capture messages that fail processing after a configurable number of delivery attempts (max_delivery_attempts). This prevents poison messages from blocking the subscription indefinitely and enables separate error-handling workflows.

Ordering keys ensure that messages with the same key are delivered in the order they were published, enabling ordered processing for related events (e.g., all updates for the same entity). Without ordering keys, Pub/Sub makes no ordering guarantees across messages.

question.title: Cost Optimization
question.scenario: A company wants to reduce Compute Engine costs for development VMs that are only used during business hours.
question.question-text: Which approach reduces costs for VMs with predictable usage patterns?

choices.choice: Schedule VMs to stop during off-hours using Cloud Scheduler and Cloud Functions
Downgrade to the smallest machine type
Use preemptible VMs for all workloads

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Compute Engine charges per second for running VMs. Stopping VMs during predictable idle periods (nights and weekends) eliminates compute charges while preserving disks and configuration.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
