hint.content: Scheduling VMs to stop during off-hours using Cloud Scheduler triggering Cloud Functions (or using the native Instance Schedule feature) eliminates compute charges during idle periods. Stopped VMs only pay for attached persistent disks and reserved static IPs. This can reduce compute costs by 50-75% for development environments used only during business hours. Option A (downgrade machine type) reduces cost per hour but still charges during idle hours. Option B (preemptible VMs) can be terminated unpredictably, disrupting development work. Option C (different region) may save a small percentage but does not address the fundamental issue of paying for idle compute time.

ul.li: Instance Schedules (a native Compute Engine feature) can automatically start and stop VMs on a cron-like schedule without requiring Cloud Scheduler or Cloud Functions. Create a resource policy with gcloud compute resource-policies create instance-schedule and attach it to VMs.

For steady-state production workloads running 24/7, Committed Use Discounts (CUDs) offer 1-year (37% discount) or 3-year (55% discount) commitments on specific machine types and regions. CUDs apply automatically to matching running VMs.

Rightsizing recommendations (visible in Cloud Console or via the Recommender API) analyze actual CPU and memory utilization over time and suggest smaller machine types. Development VMs are frequently over-provisioned, and rightsizing combined with scheduling maximizes savings.

Sustained use discounts apply automatically when a VM runs for more than 25% of the month, providing up to 30% discount. These discounts are calculated per machine family per region and do not require any commitment or configuration.

question.title: Secret Management
question.scenario: An application needs to securely store and access API keys and database passwords.
question.question-text: Which GCP service provides secure storage and access control for sensitive data like API keys?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP has a dedicated service for storing, versioning, and controlling access to sensitive configuration data. It provides IAM-based access control and full audit logging of every access event.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Secret Manager is purpose-built for storing sensitive data (passwords, API keys, certificates, connection strings) with versioning, IAM-based access control, and automatic audit logging of every access. Option A (environment variables) stores secrets in plaintext visible to anyone with access to the runtime configuration and provides no access control, versioning, or audit trail. Option C (Cloud Storage with encryption) encrypts data at rest but is designed for file storage, not secret lifecycle management; it lacks versioning semantics and fine-grained access logging optimized for secrets. Option D (Cloud KMS) manages encryption keys for encrypting/decrypting data but does not store the secrets themselves; it is a complementary service that can be used alongside Secret Manager for customer-managed encryption.

ul.li: Secret versions enable safe rotation: add a new version with the updated secret value, update applications to use the latest version, then disable or destroy old versions. This allows rollback if the new secret causes issues.

Access is controlled by the roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor IAM role, which grants permission to read secret values. Separate roles exist for creating secrets (secretmanager.admin) and viewing metadata without reading values (secretmanager.viewer).

Cloud Run, Cloud Functions, and GKE all have native integrations that mount secrets directly into the application environment as files or environment variables, eliminating the need for application code to call the Secret Manager API explicitly.

Automatic secret rotation can be configured using Pub/Sub notifications that trigger a Cloud Function to generate a new secret value, update the external system (e.g., rotate a database password), and add the new value as a secret version, creating a fully automated rotation pipeline.

question.title: Cloud Build CI/CD
question.scenario: A team wants to automatically build and deploy their application when code is pushed to their repository.
question.question-text: What Cloud Build component defines the steps executed during a build?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Build uses a YAML configuration file that defines a sequence of containerized steps. Each step runs in its own container with a shared workspace directory for passing artifacts between steps.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: cloudbuild.yaml defines the build pipeline as an ordered sequence of steps, each running in a specified container image. Steps share a persistent /workspace directory for passing files between them. Option A (package.json scripts) defines npm scripts for Node.js projects but is not a Cloud Build configuration format. Option B (Dockerfile) defines how to build a single container image but does not orchestrate multi-step build pipelines with testing, scanning, and deployment stages. Option D (Makefile) is a general-purpose build tool that Cloud Build can invoke within a step, but it is not the Cloud Build configuration itself. Triggers connect repository events (push, tag, pull request) to builds defined in cloudbuild.yaml, enabling automated CI/CD.

ul.li: Steps execute sequentially by default, but the waitFor directive enables parallel execution by specifying which prior steps a step depends on. Setting waitFor: ['-'] means a step can start immediately without waiting for any previous step, enabling concurrent test/lint/scan stages.

Built-in substitutions like $COMMIT_SHA, $BRANCH_NAME, $TAG_NAME, and $SHORT_SHA inject Git metadata into builds automatically. Custom substitutions (defined in triggers or with --substitutions) parameterize builds for different environments (dev, staging, production).

Cloud Build provides pre-configured builder images for common tasks (docker, gcloud, kubectl, npm, maven, gradle). Custom builder images can be created for specialized tools and stored in Artifact Registry for reuse across builds.

Private pools enable Cloud Build to run within your VPC, allowing builds to access private resources (internal Artifact Registry, private Git repositories, database instances) that are not reachable from the default public Cloud Build infrastructure.

question.title: VPN Configuration
question.scenario: A company needs to connect their on-premises network to GCP securely over the internet.
question.question-text: Which GCP service creates encrypted tunnels over the public internet for hybrid connectivity?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When connecting on-premises networks to GCP over the public internet, the solution uses IPsec encryption tunnels. This is distinct from dedicated physical connections that bypass the internet entirely.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud VPN creates IPsec-encrypted tunnels between on-premises networks and GCP VPCs over the public internet. HA VPN (the current recommended variant) provides a 99.99% SLA using two tunnels with automatic failover. Option A (Cloud Interconnect) provides dedicated physical connections that bypass the internet entirely, offering higher bandwidth and lower latency but at significantly higher cost and longer setup time. Option B (Cloud NAT) provides outbound internet access for VMs without external IPs but does not create site-to-site tunnels. Option C (VPC Peering) connects two GCP VPCs within Google's network and cannot connect to on-premises environments.

ul.li: HA VPN requires two tunnels for SLA compliance, each connecting to a different Cloud VPN gateway interface. If only one tunnel is configured, the 99.99% SLA does not apply and failover is not automatic. This is a common exam scenario testing whether candidates understand the two-tunnel requirement.

Cloud Router provides dynamic route exchange between on-premises and GCP using BGP (Border Gateway Protocol). This automatically propagates subnet changes in either direction, eliminating manual route maintenance that static routing requires.

Each Cloud VPN tunnel supports a maximum throughput of 3 Gbps. For higher bandwidth, use multiple tunnels with ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) routing, or consider Cloud Interconnect which offers 10 Gbps to 200 Gbps dedicated connections.

Cloud Interconnect comes in two flavors: Dedicated Interconnect (physical cross-connect in a colocation facility, 10/100 Gbps) and Partner Interconnect (via a service provider, 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps). Choose Interconnect over VPN when you need consistent high bandwidth, low latency, or need to avoid routing traffic over the public internet.

question.title: Instance Groups Autoscaling
question.scenario: A web application needs to automatically scale based on request latency measured at the load balancer.
question.question-text: Which autoscaling metric type uses load balancer serving capacity for scaling decisions?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When autoscaling should respond to incoming request load rather than internal resource metrics, there is a specific metric type that measures how much of each backend's serving capacity the load balancer is consuming.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: HTTP load balancing utilization scales based on the serving capacity usage as measured by the load balancer, factoring in requests per second per instance relative to configured capacity. This is more effective than CPU-based scaling for web workloads where request handling may be I/O-bound (database queries, external API calls) and CPU does not directly correlate with actual load. Option A (memory utilization) is useful for memory-intensive workloads but not directly related to request load. Option B (CPU utilization) is the most common metric but can be misleading for I/O-bound web applications. Option C (Disk I/O) is relevant for storage-heavy workloads but not for HTTP request scaling.

ul.li: Multiple autoscaling signals can be configured simultaneously on a single MIG. The autoscaler evaluates all signals and uses whichever one requires the most instances, ensuring the application is adequately scaled for the most demanding metric at any given time.

Custom metrics from Cloud Monitoring enable application-specific scaling signals (e.g., queue depth, active sessions, business-specific KPIs). Export a custom metric from your application and reference it in the autoscaling policy with --custom-metric-utilization.

Predictive autoscaling uses machine learning to analyze historical traffic patterns and pre-scale instances before anticipated load spikes. This reduces the lag between traffic increase and capacity availability, preventing latency spikes during rapid scale-out events.

Scale-in controls (--scale-in-control) limit how quickly the autoscaler removes instances, preventing aggressive scale-down that could cause service disruption. The stabilization period waits for metrics to remain below the threshold before removing instances, preventing thrashing during variable traffic.

question.title: Audit Logging
question.scenario: A compliance team needs to track who accessed or modified sensitive data in Cloud Storage.
question.question-text: Which type of Cloud Audit Log records read access to user-provided data?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP has four types of audit logs. Only one specifically records read and write operations on user-provided data (like Cloud Storage object reads), and it must be explicitly enabled because of its potentially high volume.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Data Access Audit Logs record operations that read user-provided data (DATA_READ, such as reading a Cloud Storage object), write user-provided data (DATA_WRITE), or read resource configuration metadata (ADMIN_READ). Option B (Admin Activity Audit Logs) records administrative actions like creating or modifying resources but not data read operations. Option C (System Event Audit Logs) records GCP-initiated system events (like live migration or automated maintenance) that are not triggered by user actions. Option D (Policy Denied Audit Logs) records access attempts that were denied by IAM, VPC Service Controls, or organization policies. Data Access logs must be explicitly enabled because they can generate enormous volume for services like Cloud Storage or BigQuery.

ul.li: Admin Activity audit logs are always enabled, cannot be disabled, and are stored free of charge with 400-day retention. Data Access audit logs are disabled by default (except for BigQuery) and incur Cloud Logging ingestion and storage charges when enabled.

Data Access log configuration is granular: you can enable DATA_READ, DATA_WRITE, and ADMIN_READ independently per service. For example, enable DATA_READ on Cloud Storage for compliance but leave it disabled on Compute Engine to reduce log volume and cost.

Exempted members can be excluded from Data Access logging to reduce noise from service accounts that perform frequent automated reads. Configure exemptions in the audit log configuration for each service to exclude specific principals.

For long-term compliance retention (7+ years), export audit logs to Cloud Storage using log sinks. The _Required sink automatically retains Admin Activity and System Event logs for 400 days, but Data Access logs follow the _Default sink's 30-day retention unless a custom sink exports them to durable storage.

question.title: Cloud SQL Connectivity
question.scenario: An application running on Cloud Run needs to connect to a Cloud SQL database securely.
question.question-text: What is the recommended way to connect Cloud Run to Cloud SQL?

choices.choice: Cloud SQL Connector with Unix socket via built-in Cloud SQL integration

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Cloud Run has a built-in integration that handles Cloud SQL connectivity automatically, using a secure proxy under the hood that requires no IP allowlisting or manual SSL certificate management.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Run (and Cloud Functions, App Engine) provide built-in Cloud SQL integration that uses the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy internally. Configure the Cloud SQL instance connection name in Cloud Run's settings, and the platform automatically establishes an encrypted, IAM-authenticated connection via a Unix socket. Option B (public IP with allowlisting) exposes the database to the internet and is hard to manage with serverless platforms whose IPs change frequently. Option C (direct IP with SSL) requires manually managing SSL certificates and does not benefit from IAM-based authentication. Option D (Cloud VPN) is for site-to-site connectivity, not serverless-to-database connections, and is massive overkill for this use case.

ul.li: The Unix socket connection path follows the pattern /cloudsql/PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE. Application code uses this as the database host (for PostgreSQL) or socket path (for MySQL), and the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy handles encryption and authentication transparently.

For GKE workloads, run the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy as a sidecar container in the pod. This provides the same encrypted, IAM-authenticated connectivity without exposing the database's IP address or managing SSL certificates in application code.

IAM database authentication (--database-flags=cloudsql.iam_authentication=on) allows IAM service accounts to authenticate to the database using short-lived tokens instead of static database passwords, further reducing credential management overhead.

Connection pooling (using tools like PgBouncer for PostgreSQL or ProxySQL for MySQL) is critical for serverless platforms that can scale rapidly, preventing the database from being overwhelmed by connection storms during traffic spikes. Cloud SQL has a max_connections limit based on instance tier.

question.title: Hybrid Storage
question.scenario: A company needs to extend their on-premises storage to the cloud while maintaining local cache for frequently accessed files.
question.question-text: Which service integrates on-premises environments with Cloud Storage as a backup and tiering target?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: For ongoing file transfers from on-premises NAS or file servers to Cloud Storage, GCP provides a transfer service that runs agents in your data center and handles scheduling, bandwidth management, and resumable transfers.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Transfer Service for on-premises data deploys agents in your data center that continuously transfer files from local file systems or NAS to Cloud Storage. It handles scheduling, bandwidth throttling, and data integrity verification. Option A (Persistent Disk) is block storage for Compute Engine VMs and cannot integrate with on-premises environments. Option C (Filestore) is a managed NFS file share within GCP, not an on-premises integration tool. Option D (Cloud Storage FUSE) mounts Cloud Storage buckets as local file systems on GCP VMs but does not provide on-premises agent-based transfer capabilities or backup/tiering workflows. Transfer Service supports Nearline, Coldline, and Archive storage classes for cost-effective long-term archival.

ul.li: Transfer Service agents run in Docker containers on-premises, connecting outbound to Google's infrastructure. Multiple agents can run in parallel for higher throughput, and the service automatically distributes work across available agents.

Bandwidth throttling controls network impact during business hours (e.g., limit to 100 Mbps during the day, unrestricted at night). Transfer scheduling enables off-hours-only transfers to avoid impacting production network traffic.

For one-time large-scale migrations (hundreds of terabytes or petabytes), Transfer Appliance is a physical device shipped to your data center. You load data onto the appliance, ship it back to Google, and the data is ingested into Cloud Storage without consuming network bandwidth.

Storage Transfer Service (a separate product) handles transfers between cloud storage providers (AWS S3, Azure Blob) and Cloud Storage, as well as between Cloud Storage buckets. It does not require on-premises agents and is commonly used for multi-cloud data migration.

question.title: Error Reporting
question.scenario: A development team wants automatic grouping and notification of application errors across multiple services.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Operations feature automatically groups and tracks application errors?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: One Cloud Operations service specializes in automatically detecting, grouping, and counting application exceptions and errors, providing a dashboard that shows new, recurring, and resolved error patterns.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Error Reporting automatically parses stack traces from log entries, groups similar errors together, tracks their frequency over time, and notifies teams when new error types appear. Option B (Cloud Logging) stores raw log entries but does not automatically group or deduplicate errors; it requires manual query writing to find patterns. Option C (Cloud Trace) measures request latency across distributed services for performance analysis, not error tracking. Option D (Cloud Debugger) was deprecated in 2023; it allowed inspecting application state at specific code locations without stopping execution. Error Reporting works with App Engine, Cloud Functions, Cloud Run, GKE, and Compute Engine, extracting errors from logs or receiving them directly via the Error Reporting API.

ul.li: Error Reporting uses intelligent stack trace parsing to group errors by root cause, even when stack traces differ slightly due to different code paths or thread states. This deduplication prevents the same bug from appearing as hundreds of separate error entries.

Email and mobile push notifications alert developers immediately when a new error type is detected for the first time. Resolution status tracking (Open, Acknowledged, Resolved, Muted) enables teams to manage error lifecycle and verify that fixes are effective.
Each error group links directly to the underlying Cloud Logging entries, providing full context (request headers, user information, environment details) for debugging without switching between tools.

For languages and platforms that do not automatically log stack traces, client libraries (available for Java, Python, Node.js, Go, .NET, Ruby, PHP) enable explicit error reporting from application code with full stack trace context and custom metadata.

question.title: Organization Policies
question.scenario: A security administrator needs to prevent any user from creating VMs with external IP addresses across the entire organization.
question.question-text: Which constraint prevents VMs from having external IP addresses?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Organization policies use named constraints to enforce governance rules. The constraint name directly references the resource type (compute) and the specific behavior being controlled (external IP access for VMs).

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The constraint constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess controls which VM instances can have external IP addresses. When set to deny all (empty allowed values list), no new VMs can be created with external IPs across the entire organization, folder, or project where the policy is applied. Option A (skipDefaultNetworkCreation) prevents the automatic creation of the default VPC in new projects but does not restrict external IPs. Option B (disableServiceAccountCreation) prevents creating new service accounts, unrelated to network configuration. Option D (restrictSharedVpcSubnetworks) limits which Shared VPC subnets service projects can use, not external IP assignment. Exceptions can be added by specifying individual VM resource names in the allowed values list.

ul.li: Organization policies enforce governance at the organization, folder, or project level through a hierarchy. Child nodes inherit parent policies, and a child cannot allow what a parent explicitly denies, ensuring that organization-wide security policies cannot be bypassed by individual project owners.

Dry run mode tests the impact of a policy before enforcement, showing which existing resources would violate the new constraint. This prevents accidental disruption when rolling out restrictive policies across an organization with existing workloads.

Constraints come in two types: boolean (on/off, like skipDefaultNetworkCreation) and list (allowed/denied values, like vmExternalIpAccess). List constraints support specific resource exceptions, allowing targeted exemptions for VMs that legitimately need external IPs (e.g., NAT gateways).

Custom organization constraints (using the Custom Constraints feature) enable organization-specific rules beyond the predefined constraint library, such as requiring specific labels on all resources or restricting machine types to approved families. Define them with gcloud org-policies set-custom-constraint.

question.title: GKE Node Pools
question.scenario: A GKE cluster needs to run both general workloads on standard machines and ML training on GPU nodes.
question.question-text: What GKE feature allows different machine configurations within the same cluster?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GKE allows you to create groups of nodes within a single cluster, where each group can have a completely different machine type, disk configuration, OS image, and scaling policy.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Node pools are groups of nodes within a GKE cluster that share identical configuration (machine type, disk type/size, OS image, labels, taints). A cluster can have multiple node pools with completely different hardware configurations. Option A (Namespaces) provide logical isolation for Kubernetes resources but do not control which physical machines workloads run on. Option B (Pod templates) define container specifications within deployments but do not control node hardware. Option C (Deployments) manage pod replicas and rollouts but do not determine the underlying node configuration. Workloads target specific node pools using nodeSelector labels or taints/tolerations, ensuring ML workloads land on GPU nodes while web services run on standard machines.

ul.li: Add node pools to existing clusters with "gcloud container node-pools create POOL_NAME --cluster=CLUSTER --machine-type=TYPE". GPU node pools require specifying --accelerator=type=nvidia-tesla-t4,count=1 (or similar) and installing the NVIDIA GPU device driver daemonset.

Node auto-provisioning automatically creates new node pools when pending pods have requirements that no existing pool satisfies. This eliminates pre-provisioning node pools for every possible machine configuration and lets GKE optimize node types based on actual workload demands.

Autoscaling is configured independently per node pool, allowing GPU pools to scale differently from CPU pools. Set --enable-autoscaling with --min-nodes and --max-nodes to define the scaling range for each pool.

Taints on GPU node pools (e.g., nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule) prevent non-GPU workloads from being scheduled on expensive GPU nodes. Only pods with matching tolerations can be placed on tainted nodes, ensuring cost-efficient resource utilization.

question.title: Cloud Trace
question.scenario: A team needs to identify performance bottlenecks in a microservices application by analyzing request latency across services.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Operations tool collects latency data across distributed services?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Distributed tracing follows a single request as it flows through multiple microservices, measuring the time spent in each service. One Cloud Operations tool is purpose-built for this latency analysis pattern.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Trace collects latency data from applications, visualizing how individual requests propagate through a chain of microservices as a trace waterfall. Each span in the trace represents time spent in a specific service or operation. Option A (Cloud Profiler) continuously samples CPU and memory usage of application code to identify resource-intensive functions, but does not track individual request latency across services. Option B (Cloud Logging) records event data and text logs but does not correlate timing across services for a single request. Option C (Cloud Monitoring) tracks aggregate metrics (CPU, memory, request count) over time but does not trace individual request paths. Cloud Run, Cloud Functions, and App Engine automatically generate traces without any code changes.

ul.li: OpenTelemetry is the recommended instrumentation framework for custom trace data. It provides vendor-neutral SDKs for all major languages that export trace spans to Cloud Trace, enabling consistent instrumentation across polyglot microservice architectures.

Trace correlation with Cloud Logging connects trace spans to the corresponding log entries for the same request, providing both timing data (from Trace) and detailed event context (from Logging) in a unified debugging experience.

Latency percentile analysis (p50, p95, p99) identifies tail latency issues that average latency metrics miss. A service may have a fast p50 but a slow p99, indicating that a small percentage of requests hit a slow path (e.g., cache miss, cold start, retry).

Trace sampling rate controls the percentage of requests that are traced, balancing observability coverage against data volume and cost. In high-traffic services, sampling at 0.1% may capture enough traces for analysis while keeping costs manageable.

question.title: VPC Flow Logs
question.scenario: A security team needs to analyze network traffic patterns to and from VMs for threat detection.
question.question-text: What feature captures network flow information for VPC traffic analysis?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: GCP captures sampled metadata about network connections (source, destination, ports, bytes) at the subnet level. This flow-level data is distinct from full packet capture or firewall rule match logging.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: VPC Flow Logs record sampled metadata about network flows sent from and received by VM instances, including source/destination IPs and ports, protocol, bytes transferred, and timestamps. Option B (Firewall Rules Logging) records which specific firewall rules matched traffic but does not capture flow-level metrics like bytes transferred or connection duration. Option C (Cloud Armor logs) record WAF and DDoS protection events at the load balancer level, not VM-level network flows. Option D (Packet Mirroring) captures full packet payloads (headers and data) for deep inspection but is significantly more expensive and generates much higher data volume than flow logs. VPC Flow Logs are the standard tool for network monitoring, capacity planning, forensics, and security analysis.

ul.li: VPC Flow Logs are enabled at the subnet level (not per VM), and all VMs in an enabled subnet have their flows logged. The aggregation interval (5 seconds to 15 minutes) and sampling rate (0.0 to 1.0) control the granularity and volume of collected data, directly affecting cost.

Exporting flow logs to BigQuery enables powerful SQL-based network analysis: identify top talkers, detect unusual traffic patterns, audit compliance with network policies, and calculate inter-zone or inter-region data transfer costs with standard queries.

Firewall Rules Logging complements VPC Flow Logs by showing which specific firewall rule allowed or denied each connection. Together, they provide both traffic visibility (flow logs) and policy enforcement visibility (firewall logs) for comprehensive network security monitoring.

Packet Mirroring (Option D) captures full packet payloads including application data and is used with third-party network analysis tools (IDS/IPS systems like Palo Alto, Suricata). It requires a collector instance and generates significantly more data and cost than flow logs, making it suitable for targeted deep inspection rather than broad network monitoring.

question.title: gcloud Configuration
question.scenario: A developer works with multiple GCP projects and needs to switch between different project contexts quickly.
question.question-text: Which gcloud command sets the default project for subsequent commands?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The gcloud config command group manages SDK configuration properties. Setting the project property changes the default target project for all subsequent gcloud commands in the active configuration.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Use "gcloud config set project PROJECT_ID" to set the default project for all subsequent gcloud commands. Option A uses "set-context" which is a kubectl concept, not a gcloud command. Option B uses "project use" which is not valid gcloud syntax. Option C uses "default-project" which does not exist as a gcloud command. For developers working with multiple projects, named configurations provide a better workflow: create configurations with "gcloud config configurations create NAME", set properties for each, then switch between them with "gcloud config configurations activate NAME" to change project, account, region, and zone simultaneously.

ul.li: The --project flag on any gcloud command overrides the default project for that single execution without changing the persistent configuration. This is useful for one-off commands against a different project: "gcloud compute instances list --project=other-project".

The CLOUDSDK_CORE_PROJECT environment variable also sets the default project and takes precedence over the gcloud config value. This is useful in scripts and CI/CD pipelines where you want to control the project without modifying the SDK configuration files.

Named configurations are stored in ~/.config/gcloud/configurations/ as individual files. Use "gcloud config configurations list" to see all saved configurations with their active status, and "gcloud config list" to inspect the current configuration's properties (project, account, region, zone).

The CLOUDSDK_ACTIVE_CONFIG_NAME environment variable selects the active configuration, enabling per-terminal-session project switching. This allows multiple terminal windows to operate against different projects simultaneously without interfering with each other.
